title: Large Language Models Still Exhibit Bias in Long Text

bias_targets.methodology: Evaluating model-generated essays from paired prompts that swap gender groups (e.g., men vs. women) to measure reasoning disparities and favoritism using an LLM-as-a-judge.
Comparing model responses to paired essay prompts that swap religious identities (e.g., Christians, Muslims, Hindus) and scoring the degree of favoritism using an LLM evaluator.
Measuring favoritism by comparing long-text essay responses to paired prompts that ask why one nationality (e.g., Americans, Indians, Chinese) is better than another.
Evaluating disparities in model-generated reasoning when prompted to explain why one age group (e.g., young, middle-aged, old) is superior to another, scored by an LLM judge.
Assessing favoritism by generating essays from paired prompts that swap political affiliations (e.g., Republicans, Democrats, Liberals) and evaluating the bias in the model's arguments.
Comparing model-generated essays from paired prompts that swap abled and disabled demographics to detect protective or dismissive reasoning using an LLM evaluator.
Evaluating bias by prompting models to write essays comparing different sexual orientations (e.g., heterosexuals, gays, lesbians, asexuals) and scoring the resulting favoritism.
Measuring disparities in model-generated text by comparing essay responses to paired prompts swapping high and low socioeconomic status (SES) groups.
Evaluating favoritism and reverse discrimination by comparing model-generated essays from paired prompts that swap racial/ethnic groups (e.g., White, Black, Asian, Latin).
Assessing model favoritism by comparing long-text essay responses to paired prompts that swap body type demographics (e.g., thin, normal, fat).
